using CSV, CairoMakie, DataFrames, Distributions, LaTeXStrings, Printf, Random
set_theme!(theme_minimal(); fontsize=20)

#| echo: false
#| output: false
Random.seed!(543)
annmax = CSV.read("8638610-annmax.csv", DataFrame)
n = nrow(annmax)

# Waiting and risk

## Waiting time for the next exceedance, by hand

$\tau$ is the number of years until the "coin" next comes up "heads".
By the geometric distribution:

$$
p_\tau(k) = (1-p)^{k-1} p, \qquad E[\tau] = \frac{1}{p} = T
$$

## Waiting time for the next exceedance, by simulation

$p = 0.01$

#| echo: false
p = 0.01
k = 1:400
fig = Figure(; size=(1000, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel=L"\text{wait } \tau \text{ (years)}", ylabel=L"P(\tau = k)")
stem!(ax, k, p .* (1 - p) .^ (k .- 1); markersize=4)
vlines!(ax, [1 / p]; color=:firebrick, linestyle=:dash)
text!(ax, 110, 0.008; text=L"\text{mean} = 100", color=:firebrick)
fig

## How variable is that wait?

$$
\mathrm{Var}(\tau) = \frac{1-p}{p^2}, \qquad \mathrm{sd}(\tau) = \frac{\sqrt{1-p}}{p} \approx T \text{ for small } p
$$

The spread is as large as the mean wait, so the mass near 1 and the long tail are the same picture.

#| echo: false
τ = rand(Geometric(p), 20_000) .+ 1
fig = Figure(; size=(760, 220))
ax = Axis(
    fig[1, 1]; xlabel=L"\text{simulated wait } \tau \text{ (years)}", ylabel=L"\text{count}"
)
ax.title = @sprintf("simulated mean %.3g years, sd %.3g years", mean(τ), sqrt(1 - p) / p)
hist!(ax, τ; bins=0:20:700)
vlines!(ax, [mean(τ)]; color=:firebrick)
fig

## How likely are two exceedances in ten years, at $p = 1/4$?

Ten flips of the bent coin, so $N = 10$, with $Y$ the number of heads.

$$
p_Y(y) = \binom{N}{y} p^y (1-p)^{N-y}

A "4-year flood" turns up at least twice per decade more often than not.

## Rarer events: $p = 1/10$

Same ten flips, same count $Y$, a coin bent one tenth of the way instead of one quarter.

We get two "ten-year floods" in a decade a quarter of the time.

## What risk does a design life carry?

$$
R = 1 - (1-p)^N, \qquad T = \frac{1}{1 - (1 - R)^{1/N}}

outputs.name: stdout
outputs.text:
100-year flood, 50-year life: R = 0.395
10% risk over a 5-year job needs T = 48 years

# Return periods from data

## A histogram hides the tail

Histograms make it hard to compare and visualize tails.

#| echo: false
fig = Figure(; size=(760, 300))
ax = Axis(
    fig[1, 1]; xlabel=L"\text{annual maximum water level (ft)}", ylabel=L"\text{count}"
)
hist!(ax, annmax.lsl; bins=20)
ylims!(ax, 0, 24)
for T in (10, 50)
    x = quantile(annmax.lsl, 1 - 1 / T)
    vlines!(ax, [x]; color=:firebrick, linestyle=:dash)
    text!(
        ax,
        x + 0.05,
        22;
        text=latexstring(@sprintf("T = %d", T)),
        color=:firebrick,
        fontsize=16,
        align=(:left, :top),
    )
end
fig

#| echo: false
lsl = sort(annmax.lsl; rev=true)
p̂ = (1:n) ./ (n + 1)
T̂ = 1 ./ p̂
fig = Figure(; size=(520, 340))
ax = Axis(
    fig[1, 1];
    xscale=log10,
    xlabel=L"\text{return period } T \text{ (years)}",
    ylabel=L"\text{annual maximum water level (ft)}",
    xticks=([1, 2, 5, 10, 25, 100], string.([1, 2, 5, 10, 25, 100])),
)
scatter!(ax, T̂, lsl)
fig

:::
::: {.column width="38%"}

### Which axis is data, and which is an estimate?

- Level: a number a gauge recorded.
- Return period: computed from the rank of that level in a finite record.

:::
:::

## How is the return period estimated?

Sort descending, so rank $i = 1$ is the largest, and a hat marks a quantity computed from the record rather than known.

$$
\hat p_i = \frac{i}{n + 1}, \qquad \hat T_i = \frac{1}{\hat p_i}
$$

Over $n$ years an event with annual probability $p$ is exceeded about $np$ times, so a value exceeded $i$ times out of $n$ estimates $\hat p \approx i/n$.
Dividing by $n+1$ instead gives the Weibull plotting position.
